title: Fever in children under 5: assessment and initial management
subject: paediatrics
setting: Primary care, emergency department, paediatric ward
summary: Check every febrile child under 5 for life-threatening features and the NICE traffic light signs; infants under 3 months with 38 °C or more are high risk. Investigate and treat by risk, give parenteral ceftriaxone if shocked, unrousable or meningococcal, and use antipyretics only for distress.

sections.title: Life-threatening and red (high-risk) features
items: First identify immediately life-threatening features (airway, breathing, circulation, reduced consciousness) and ask 'could this be sepsis?' (NICE sepsis guideline).

Red: pale, mottled, ashen or blue; no response to social cues, appears ill to a clinician, does not wake or stay awake, weak, high-pitched or continuous cry; grunting, respiratory rate above 60, moderate or severe chest indrawing; reduced skin turgor.
Also red: age under 3 months with temperature 38 °C or more, non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, status epilepticus, focal neurological signs or focal seizures.

Amber (intermediate): pallor reported by carer, not responding normally to social cues, no smile, wakes only with prolonged stimulation, decreased activity, nasal flaring, SpO2 95% or less in air, crackles, respiratory rate above 50 (6 to 12 months) or above 40 (over 12 months).

Also amber: heart rate above 160 (under 12 months), above 150 (12 to 24 months) or above 140 (2 to 5 years); capillary refill 3 seconds or more; dry mucous membranes, poor feeding, reduced urine output; age 3 to 6 months with 39 °C or more; fever 5 days or more; rigors; limb or joint swelling or not using a limb.

Green (low risk): normal colour, responds normally to social cues, content or smiling, stays awake or wakes quickly, strong normal cry or not crying, normal skin and eyes, moist mucous membranes, and no amber or red feature.

Record temperature (electronic axillary thermometer under 4 weeks; axillary or infrared tympanic at 4 weeks to 5 years), heart rate, respiratory rate and capillary refill in every child. Take parental report of fever seriously; do not use forehead strips.

sections.title: Look for a source
items: Meningococcal disease: fever with non-blanching rash, especially if ill-looking, purpura over 2 mm, capillary refill 3 seconds or more, or neck stiffness. Meningitis: neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, reduced consciousness or convulsive status; classic signs are often absent in infants.
Herpes simplex encephalitis: focal neurological signs, focal seizures or reduced consciousness.
Pneumonia: respiratory rate above 60 (0 to 5 months), above 50 (6 to 12 months) or above 40 (over 12 months), crackles, nasal flaring, chest indrawing, cyanosis, SpO2 95% or less.

UTI: consider it in every febrile child under 5 and test urine (see the Urinary tract infection in children protocol). Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis: swollen limb or joint, not using a limb, not weight bearing.

Kawasaki disease: fever 5 days or more with bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection, red cracked lips or strawberry tongue, oedema or redness of hands and feet, polymorphous rash, or cervical lymphadenopathy. Infants under 1 year may show fewer features but have higher coronary risk.

sections.title: Immediate treatment (ED or paediatric specialist)
items: Shock: IV or IO bolus of 10 mL/kg glucose-free crystalloid (sodium 130 to 154 mmol/L) over less than 10 minutes (max 250 mL). Reassess; if no better, give a second bolus, then call a consultant to attend (NICE sepsis).

Give parenteral antibiotics immediately if shocked, unrousable or showing signs of meningococcal disease; consider them with reduced consciousness. Do the lumbar puncture first only if it causes no delay.

Antibiotic: ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg IV once daily (max 4 g) from 28 days of age. Under 3 months, add amoxicillin or ampicillin to cover Listeria. Neonates under 28 days: see the Neonatal sepsis protocol.
Suspected meningococcal disease outside hospital: give IM or IV benzylpenicillin or a third-generation cephalosporin at the earliest opportunity, before transfer.
Suspected herpes simplex encephalitis: add IV aciclovir.
Oxygen if shocked or SpO2 below 92% in air; consider it above 92% if clinically indicated.
Do not prescribe oral antibiotics to a child with fever without an apparent source.

sections.title: Investigations by age and risk
items: Under 3 months: observe and record temperature, heart rate and respiratory rate. Do FBC, blood culture, CRP and urine testing; chest X-ray only with respiratory signs; stool culture if diarrhoea.

Lumbar puncture (unless contraindicated) and parenteral antibiotics for: all infants under 1 month, infants 1 to 3 months who look unwell, and infants 1 to 3 months with WBC below 5 or above 15 x 10^9/L.
3 months and over, any red feature, no source: FBC, blood culture, CRP and urine; consider lumbar puncture, chest X-ray, electrolytes and blood gas as guided by the assessment.

Amber feature, no source: urine, FBC, CRP and blood culture unless an experienced paediatrician judges them unnecessary; consider lumbar puncture under 1 year; chest X-ray if temperature above 39 °C and WBC above 20 x 10^9/L.
Green: test urine and assess for pneumonia; do not routinely do blood tests or chest X-ray.
Proven RSV or influenza does not exclude serious bacterial infection: still assess for red and amber features and consider urine testing.

sections.title: Antipyretics and comfort
items: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures and should not be used for that purpose, nor solely to lower the temperature.

If the child is distressed, give paracetamol or ibuprofen; continue only while distressed and switch to the other if distress persists. Do not give both at once; alternate only if distress persists or recurs before the next dose is due.
Do not use tepid sponging; do not underdress or over-wrap the child.
A fall, or no fall, in temperature after an antipyretic does not separate serious from minor illness. Reassess children with amber or red features after 1 to 2 hours regardless.
Offer regular fluids (breast milk if breastfed) and teach carers the signs of dehydration: sunken fontanelle, dry mouth, sunken eyes, no tears, poor overall appearance.

sections.title: Disposition and safety netting
items: Remote assessment: life-threatening features, emergency ambulance; any red feature, face-to-face assessment within 2 hours; amber, face-to-face assessment with urgency by judgement; green, home care with advice.
Non-paediatric clinician: red features, urgent referral to paediatrics; amber with no diagnosis, a safety net or referral; green, home with advice.

When deciding on admission, also weigh social circumstances, parental anxiety and instinct, repeated attendance, contact with serious infection, recent travel, and illness lasting longer than expected.

Safety net: return if the child has a fit, develops a non-blanching rash, seems less well, the carer is more worried, fever lasts 5 days or more, or the carer cannot cope. Check the child during the night.
Shocked, unrousable or meningococcal disease: urgent review by an experienced paediatrician and consider PICU referral.

sections.title: India and tropical settings
items: NICE was written for the UK, where it advises asking about travel. In India, test early for malaria, dengue, enteric fever, scrub typhus and leptospirosis according to season and local epidemiology, and follow national programme protocols.
Fever with bleeding, shock, jaundice, altered sensorium or seizures needs the specific protocol (dengue, malaria, acute encephalitis syndrome, septic shock) in parallel with this one.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Judging severity by the height of the temperature (after 6 months) or its duration alone.
Assuming meningitis is excluded in an infant because neck stiffness or a bulging fontanelle is absent.
Not testing urine in a febrile child with no obvious source.
Discharging a child with amber features without a clear safety net or follow-up.
Some vaccines cause fever in infants under 3 months, but the traffic light system still classes 38 °C or more at that age as high risk: assess fully.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg orally every 4 to 6 hours when distressed (max 4 doses and 60 mg/kg in 24 hours; max 1 g per dose)
drugs.notes: For distress, not to lower the temperature or prevent seizures.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen
drugs.dose: 10 mg/kg orally every 6 to 8 hours (max 30 mg/kg/day; max 400 mg per dose)
drugs.notes: From 3 months of age. Avoid if dehydrated or if dengue is possible.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: 80 mg/kg IV once daily (max 4 g/day), age 28 days and over
drugs.notes: Community-acquired sepsis or serious bacterial infection. Neonates under 28 days: 50 mg/kg once daily, or cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6 to 12 hours if 40 weeks corrected age or less or on IV calcium (NICE).

drugs.name: Ampicillin or amoxicillin (IV)
drugs.dose: Infants 1 to 3 months: 50 mg/kg IV every 6 hours (max 2 g per dose); use meningitic dosing if meningitis is suspected
drugs.notes: Listeria cover in infants under 3 months, with ceftriaxone. Neonatal doses: see Neonatal sepsis protocol.

drugs.name: Benzylpenicillin (pre-hospital)
drugs.dose: Single IM or IV dose: under 1 year 300 mg; 1 to 9 years 600 mg; 10 years and over 1.2 g
drugs.notes: Suspected meningococcal disease before transfer; do not delay transfer.

drugs.name: Aciclovir
drugs.dose: IV every 8 hours: 20 mg/kg under 3 months; 500 mg/m2 at 3 months to 11 years
drugs.notes: Suspected herpes simplex encephalitis. Keep well hydrated; adjust for renal impairment.

drugs.name: Crystalloid bolus
drugs.dose: 10 mL/kg IV or IO over less than 10 minutes (max 250 mL); reassess, may repeat once
drugs.notes: Glucose-free, sodium 130 to 154 mmol/L. Smaller volumes with heart or kidney disease.
